reverse_outline.summary: Chapter promise: who decides what among product, engineering and design at three levels, and how to spot the three ways this breaks.
Key points: one accountable role per risk, the triad is a decision right repeated at every level, and it fails in three recognizable forms.
Which of the book's failure patterns this chapter addresses: the Feature Factory seen inside a team and the Escalation Ladder caused by a group lacking product and design leads.
Opening case: a Corvane team shipped a feature on time with all three roles present, yet none of them was asked the question it could answer.

(1) The chapter's thesis: the three roles work as a triad, each judging one risk after consulting the others, at every level, with three failure forms. (2) The roadmap of the chapter's sections in order.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: One Feature, Three Roles ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Background of the skills-matrix feature: it came from a customer-promise roadmap and was decided before the Dispatch team saw it.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: One Feature, Three Roles ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: How each role worked in sequence: the product manager wrote tickets, engineers estimated and cut the key part to hold the date, the designer only polished at the end.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene: One Feature, Three Roles ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The outcome: delivered on time but unused, because nobody judged whether the reduced feature was worth building.
Cagan's four product risks defined, and how this book folds them into three questions (value with viability, feasibility extended to running).
Each risk is assigned to one role, and those three roles (product manager, engineering lead, designer) form the triad; terminology clarified.
Accountability means deciding in your own area after consulting the other two; a table lays out risk, decision and required consultation per member.
Why the split: each risk needs different knowledge, so one person deciding all three decides two blind, as the Dispatch product manager did.
How three judgments become one decision: all three must accept their risk, and a refusal must state the condition for a yes.
The triad is a decision right, not a meeting; the weekly sync is only where the right gets exercised and can exist without it.
How the triad fits the earlier leaders-versus-team decision line: that line divides levels, the triad divides functions within a level.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Same Triad at Three Levels ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The three risks exist wherever product decisions are made, so the triad recurs at team, group and executive level, with each function coaching its role one level down.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Same Triad at Three Levels ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Only the object of the decision differs by level; a table shows what is decided at each level from the top down.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Same Triad at Three Levels ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Disclosure of source support: the books back joint leadership above the team but not the risk assignment there, which is the author's extension.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Same Triad at Three Levels ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: A test from the grid: a level missing one of the three is incomplete, and its unjudged risk is either judged blind or pushed upward.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Appoint the Three Together and Name Each Risk ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Four steps for installing the triad in one team: appoint together, name each one's risk, fill in the decision table, and do discovery jointly.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Appoint the Three Together and Name Each Risk ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: An agreed joint-escalation rule (time-boxed, shared document, commit to the answer) for disagreements the table does not resolve.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Appoint the Three Together and Name Each Risk ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: (1) Who uses the team pattern. (2) How to tell it worked: all three name the same decider, and late rework falls.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Set Up the Triad at Group Level ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Why groups usually start with only one of the three: they are created inside the engineering line, leaving product and design questions unanswered at that level.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Set Up the Triad at Group Level ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Five steps to complete a group's triad: list cross-team decisions, name product and design leads, appoint the three together, write who decides, agree escalation.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Pattern: Set Up the Triad at Group Level ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: (1) Who uses the group pattern. (2) How to tell it worked: cross-team questions settle within the group, measured by how many reach executives and how long they wait.
First failure form: product as order-giver, the Feature Factory inside the team, in two variants (relaying or choosing the solution alone).
Second failure form: engineering reduced to estimating or refusing because it sees the solution only once specified.
Third failure form: design consulted after the flow is fixed, made likely by staffing design as a shared service.
The three forms compared in a table; they share one correction, finding the solution together from a stated problem.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Where the Sources Disagree: One Owner or Three ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The opposing single-owner view and the support it gets from the author's own sources: shared accountability is feared to be none.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Where the Sources Disagree: One Owner or Three ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The triad's reply: the product manager owns the outcome but does not judge the other two risks, and each risk still has a single judge.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: A Group Triad at Corvane ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The starting state of one Corvane group in 2026: a director only, product questions queuing at the CPO and inconsistent design across its apps.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: A Group Triad at Corvane ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: How the group level was completed: product and design leads named, appointed with the director, and a one-page decision table written.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: A Group Triad at Corvane ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The first decision made under the new arrangement, showing each lead judging its own risk, including a conditional no.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Worked Example: A Group Triad at Corvane ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Results two quarters on (far fewer escalations, consistent design) together with what the change cost in people's time.
(1) The book's convention of labelling AI claims by evidence level. (2) An Emerging observation that coding agents let each role do part of the others' work.
A Speculative claim that the three accountabilities survive even if roles merge, with what evidence would confirm it.
What the sources agree on: risks have responsible roles, the three find solutions together, peers escalate jointly.
What varies by situation: who the engineering member is, whether group leads are full-time, and how much design a team needs.
What is the author's own position: the decision-right framing, the extension to upper levels, the conditional no and the named failure forms.
(1) A synthesis tying risks, levels, patterns and failure forms into one idea of three informed judgments. (2) Eight checks to run on one's own team and group.

(1) Return to the opening case as all three failure forms at once, and what a leader should do about it. (2) Hand-off: since each level needs a triad, the number of levels matters, the next chapter's topic.

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 39 aligned units: the outliner's summary states the controlling idea of the spec paragraph it is aligned to (p01-p39, with the anti-patterns in the spec's order p24, p25, p26, p23). The three callouts match no spec paragraph, by house format. The one unit that carries more than its spec paragraph is Checklist ¶1 (see one_controlling_idea_per_paragraph).

Of the six units marked two_ideas, five are by design: Introduction ¶2 (thesis plus roadmap, p02 covers both), the two pattern closings (user plus outcome measure, p19 and p22 cover both), What AI Changes Here ¶1 (one sentence of label scheme before the Emerging claim, house format) and Checklist ¶2 (callback, so-what and hand-off, all in p39's controlling idea). All other units hold one idea.

results.quote: The risks, the levels, the patterns and the failure forms are one idea: a product decision needs three judgments, each made by the one role that has the knowledge, wherever such decisions are made.
results.finding: The unit aligned to p38 holds two ideas and p38's controlling idea covers only one ("Eight checks let the reader find the triad, or its absence"). The chapter's synthesis (three sentences) stands as the lead-in to the checklist, under the Checklist heading. The spec places the synthesis in the closing paragraph p39 (its controlling idea opens with "A product decision needs three judgments at every level", and its transition introduces "the chapter's synthesis"). Move the three synthesis sentences to the start of the closing paragraph, or above the Checklist heading, and leave the checklist with its one-line lead-in.

Every unit supports the supporting claim its section declares: scene and anti-patterns S5; three-risks S1 and S2; levels S3; the two patterns S4 (group also S3); sources section S2 and S5; worked example S3 and S4; AI section S1 and S2; the conclusion units restate them. The one clause that traces to no claim is the coaching sentence in The Same Triad at Three Levels ¶1, recorded under flow_is_followable.

Every evidence item in the spec is present in its aligned unit and the draft says what it shows. Tables (who decides, levels, failure forms, the group's page) and Figure 1 are each introduced with what they give; the Cagan quotation is attributed and used; the Corvane numbers (41, 23, 26, 14, nine days, 3) agree with the spec. Small omissions that do not weaken a claim: "38 of 41 shipped by the promised date" (p05) and the second group measure, a cross-team task working one way (p22), which the worked example carries. Note, not a failure: in the team pattern's step 1 the two cited books support design as a peer inside the team, not the timing of the appointment that the step is about (flow-B 3.10); the reason for the timing is the author's own and is given in the lead-in.

All declared transitions are expressed at their boundary. Examples: p02 problem_solution ("This chapter says how the three should share decisions"), three-risks ("What nobody judged has a name"), p09 cause_effect ("divided this way because"), p11 conclusion_summary ("therefore a decision right"), pattern-group similarity ("One level up, the same setup"), p25 cause_effect ("follows from an order"), sources section ("The first of those forms ... has a respectable view behind it"), p28 contrast ("keeps what is right in that view and refuses its conclusion"), p34 contrast ("is not the same as judging its risk"). Two are expressed weakly but are readable: p05 opens with sequence ("The feature shipped in September") and gives the cause only in its last sentence; the AI section's transition is its second sentence, after the label convention.

results.draft_locus: Where the Sources Disagree: One Owner or Three ¶2
results.quote: The skills matrix shows what the single-owner conclusion produces: one role decided all three risks, two of them without the information.
results.finding: The chapter gives two incompatible accounts of the Dispatch product manager. Here and in Three Risks ¶4 ("they settled what was valuable, what was feasible and how the screen would work, and only the first was hers to know") she is one role that decided all three risks, with value hers. In the scene ("The decision to build was made before the team saw it"), in Anti-Patterns ¶1 (she is the backlog clerk who passes on a solution chosen by someone else) and in the failure-forms table (value unjudged, the request stands in for the judgment) she decided nothing. Both flow readers went back to other sections and stayed unsure whether the skills matrix is a fair case of the single-owner view. The contradiction is in the spec's evidence: p09 and p28 say the product manager decided all three risks, p05, p24 and p23 say value was judged by nobody. The author has to decide which reading holds (for example: the tickets fixed all three risks without anyone judging any of them, which is what a single owner without the knowledge also does), then p09 and p28 are reworded.

results.draft_locus: Worked Example: A Group Triad at Corvane ¶2
results.quote: Priya Nambiar named the Dispatch team's product manager as the group's product lead
results.finding: The only Dispatch product manager the reader has met is the one who wrote the 23 tickets in 2024 and was just named the backlog clerk. The draft does not say whether the 2026 product lead is the same person, and both readers stopped on it and were left unsure (both called it minor, both rated it (a), so it counts by the rule). The spec does not settle the fact either (p30 says only "the Dispatch team's product manager, who gave up her team"). One clause fixes it once the author decides: the same person four years on, or a successor.

results.draft_locus: Worked Example: A Group Triad at Corvane ¶2
results.quote: The three listed the first quarter's cross-team decisions and wrote one page.
results.finding: The example is announced as showing the second pattern, whose step 1 is to list the cross-team decisions first, because the list shows whether the two roles are needed. Here the leads are named and appointed first and make the list afterwards. Reported by flow-A only (A2, rated (a)); real. The spec's p30 does not mention the list; the draft added it in the wrong place. Have the two heads list the decisions (the fourteen questions) before they name the leads.

results.draft_locus: The Same Triad at Three Levels ¶1
results.quote: Each function also coaches its own role one level down, as the figure shows.
results.finding: Coaching is introduced here and in the figure's vertical links and is never used again (not in the levels table, the patterns, the example or the checklist). Both readers reported it; flow-B rated it (a), flow-A (b), so it is not corroborated as blocking. The clause comes from p13's controlling idea ("each function coaches and sets standards for its own role one level down"), which no other spec paragraph picks up. Either cut it and say only that each function's line runs down a column, or say in one sentence why it matters for decision rights.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Appoint the Three Together and Name Each Risk ¶2
results.quote: The table will not settle every disagreement, so the three agree beforehand how to escalate.
results.finding: The team pattern is announced as four steps and the escalation agreement follows as a paragraph outside the list, while the group pattern has the same act as step 5. Readers were unsure whether escalation is part of the first pattern (flow-B 3.4 rated (a), flow-A B8 rated (b); not corroborated as blocking). A wording fix is enough: announce "four steps and one agreement", or say that this is the pattern's last part.

results.quote: The grouping of value with viability is Cagan's own
results.finding: The paragraph before says "This book takes the first and the last together as one question" and then "that addition is mine", so the reader files the grouping as the author's; one paragraph later it is Cagan's. Both readers re-read (both (b)). Say in the first of the two paragraphs that the grouping follows Cagan's assignment of roles.

results.quote: Chapter 12's line runs between levels and the triad's lines run between functions at one level
results.finding: "Chapter 12" appears without having been tied to the chapter cited by link two sentences earlier; both readers had to infer it (both (b)). Name the chapter number where the link is given, or write "that chapter's line".

results.draft_locus: The Same Triad at Three Levels ¶4
results.quote: The team level has its own form, which [[team-size-and-composition]] counted at Corvane: seven designers for eleven teams in 2024.
results.finding: "Its own form" has no clear antecedent; both readers went back to see that it means the team-level form of a missing member, a team without a full designer (both (b)). Say that directly.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Set Up the Triad at Group Level ¶1
results.quote: Product questions that cross the group's teams climb to the head of product, and design questions that cross them are answered team by team.
results.finding: The origin and effect of the director-only group is told twice, here and at the end of the levels section ("go to the head of product, and design questions that cross them go to nobody"), with a different ending for the design questions. Both readers checked whether something new was being said (both (b)). The repetition and the two endings are in the spec (p16 evidence and p20 evidence). Keep the full account here and one sentence in the levels section, with one wording for the design questions.

Terms are defined at or before first use in the body: the four risks, triad, engineering lead, decision right, group, discovery (in step 4), Feature Factory, backlog clerk and mini-CEO, technical veto theatre, dispatch board. Callout terms (Feature Factory, Escalation Ladder, decision right) are page format and link to their definitions; evidence labels, AI labels and Corvane are explained in the book's introduction. Small slips, each reported by one reader and resolved in place: "the two roles" one step before they are named (group pattern step 1), "users" for the pattern's users after it has meant the product's users, "Corvane's platform director" unintroduced. The "Chapter 12" reference is recorded under flow_is_followable.
The opening is a specific scenario (September 2024, the Dispatch team's skills matrix) followed by the reader's own experience and the thesis; none of the weak patterns.

The conclusion sorts the claims by how settled they are, gives the synthesis, the checks, the callback and the hand-off. No new subtopic (the cost of an added level is the declared hand-off), no body evidence, not a rephrased thesis only.

Synthesis is stated ("one idea: a product decision needs three judgments, each made by the one role that has the knowledge"; patterns put a judge in each place, failure forms are a role present without its judgment) and the so-what is stated in the closing paragraph (appoint the three together at every level, name each risk, read a missing member as an incomplete structure, not a saving). Its placement under the Checklist heading is recorded under one_controlling_idea_per_paragraph.
The closing paragraph returns to the skills matrix of 2024 as the spec declares: three roles and none of the judgments; tickets, cut and polish as the three failure forms in one feature.

The cold intro reader predicted all eight sections in the order they arrive, the thesis, the three levels and the three failure forms. Two gaps, neither a failure: the roadmap sentence does not mention the fit with chapter 12's line (part of the spec's second promise), and nothing in the opening tells the reader that named sources (Cagan, Empowered, Build What Matters, Larson) will be used, so the reader expected only the fictional case and reasoning.

The cold reader named product as order-giver as the form that starts it, with design as decoration (and engineering as veto) following from it, and gave the expected correction: the three find the solution together from a stated problem, before the solution is fixed, each judging its own risk, with engineers in discovery and the designer testing the flow before it is built. Matches the criterion's expected answer.

Three Risks ¶7 states the fit: chapter 12's line runs between levels (leaders decide problems, order and measure; the team decides the solution), the triad divides the team's side among three roles, the two divisions "cross and do not compete", and above the team the same functions divide the leaders' side. The chapter is linked.

Sources are named with their concept: Cagan's article "The Four Big Risks" (four risks, role per risk, overall accountability, quoted), Empowered (leaders shape the topology together; design not run as a service), Build What Matters (Feature Factory; design as peer; one accountable person), Larson's Primer (peer functions; the five-day joint escalation, presented as Larson's and credited to LinkedIn). Extensions are marked as the author's: "and run", the last two table columns, the risks above the team, the escalation rule below executive level, the rule that a no carries its condition, the decision-right reading, the failure forms, the observation on how groups form. Two blemishes below the bar for a failure: the order of the grouping attribution (recorded under flow_is_followable) and "my record adds" in the sources section without the record's name (right-team).

Both patterns close with users and a measure. Team pattern: the three leads and the managers who appoint them; each of the three names the same decider for an open question, and late cuts, redesigns and rebuilds per quarter fall. Group pattern: the three heads and the group's teams; cross-team questions reach an executive only as joint escalations, counted per quarter with their waiting time. The worked example reports the group measure (fourteen to three).
